opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really healthy sign, honestly. What it tells you is that there's a huge amount of demand for writing fast kernels, and the traditional way of doing it, writing raw CUDA, managing shared memory and registers and synchronization by hand, is just too hard for most people and too slow even for experts. So you see this explosion: Triton, which was sort of the first one to really take off, and then things like ThunderKittens, CuTe DSL from NVIDIA, TileLang, Mojo, and a bunch of others. Everyone is trying to find the right level of abstraction.

The way I think about it is that there's a trade-off between productivity and control. Triton made it dramatically easier to write a reasonably fast kernel. You think in terms of blocks or tiles, and the compiler handles a lot of the low-level details. That's great for getting, say, 80 or 90 percent of peak performance quickly. But on the newest hardware, Hopper and now Blackwell, there are features like asynchronous memory copies with TMA, warp-specialized pipelines, the new tensor core instructions, and getting that last chunk of performance often requires controlling those things very explicitly. So you get DSLs that sit a bit lower, closer to the hardware, but still much nicer than raw CUDA C++.

For FlashAttention 3 and later work we spent a lot of time at that lower level, and one lesson is that the abstraction that matters most is the tile, a chunk of data you load, compute on, and write back. Almost all of these languages converge on that idea, and they differ in how much they expose about memory hierarchy and scheduling.

I also think it reflects the hardware landscape diversifying. It's not just NVIDIA anymore. You have AMD, and various accelerator startups, and people want to write a kernel once and have it run reasonably well across different chips. A good DSL can be a portability layer in a way that hand-tuned CUDA never was.

And then, increasingly, there's an AI angle. If you want language models to help write kernels, and we're starting to see that work, a cleaner, higher-level language with fewer footguns makes it much easier for a model to generate correct, fast code. So I expect some consolidation eventually, a few of these will win, but right now we're in the exploration phase, and that's exactly where we should be given how fast the hardware and workloads are changing.

r001.rationale: It says developers are still trying to find the right level of abstraction and calls the current period an exploration phase.

r002.rationale: It says raw CUDA is too hard for most people, but does not identify the difficulty of training engineers as a motivation.

r003.rationale: It describes ongoing exploration amid changing hardware and workloads, but does not attribute the proliferation to rapid iteration on abstractions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually a healthy sign, even though from the outside it can look like fragmentation. If you look at what's happened over the last couple of years, you have Triton, you have things like CUTLASS and CuTe evolving into Python-facing DSLs, you have ThunderKittens, Pallas on the JAX side, Mojo, a bunch of others. And the question people ask is, why do we need all of these? Why not just write CUDA?

The way I interpret it is that the hardware got hard enough that the old abstraction broke. When I was writing the first FlashAttention, you could kind of think about a GPU as a bunch of threads, you write your kernel, you reason about shared memory and registers, and that model mostly worked. With Hopper and now Blackwell, that's not true anymore. You have tensor cores that are asynchronous, you have TMA for moving data, you have warp specialization where some warps are producers and some are consumers, you have clusters, you have this whole choreography you have to get right to hit even sixty or seventy percent of peak. And writing that in raw CUDA is really painful. FlashAttention-3 was a lot of effort largely because of that.

So the DSLs are all different bets on where the right level of abstraction is. Triton's bet is: you program at the level of tiles, the compiler handles the thread mapping, and you give up some control for a lot of productivity. That's been enormously successful, a lot of people who would never write CUDA now write kernels. Something like ThunderKittens or the CuTe-style approach is a different bet: keep the programmer in control of the layout and the scheduling, but give them good primitives so they're not reinventing the same tiled matmul every time. And that matters because for the kernels that actually dominate your training or inference bill, attention and the GEMMs and increasingly the MoE routing stuff, you want that last twenty or thirty percent, and you can't always get it when the compiler is making decisions for you.

The other thing I'd say is that the proliferation reflects that we don't know the answer yet. In a mature field you'd have converged on one or two things, the way most people just use NumPy or PyTorch for the high-level stuff. Here, the hardware is changing every eighteen months, the workloads are changing, so people keep trying new points in the design space. I expect a lot of consolidation. Some of these will die, some will merge, and the ideas from the ones that die will show up in the survivors.

And then honestly the thing I'm watching most closely is what happens when models start writing a lot of these kernels. If an LLM is doing the authoring, the tradeoffs change. You might care less about how pleasant the language is for a human and more about whether it's easy to verify correctness, whether it's easy to search over the space of schedules. That could push toward lower-level, more explicit DSLs rather than higher-level ones, which is kind of the opposite of where things have been going. So I don't think of it as a mess. I think of it as a field actively figuring out what the right interface to this very weird hardware is.

r001.rationale: The response says the field does not yet know the right answer and is still figuring out the right interface for GPU hardware.

r002.rationale: It mentions raw CUDA is painful and DSLs improve productivity, but does not identify the difficulty of training engineers to write high-performance kernels as a motivation.

r003.rationale: It ties continued experimentation with DSLs to rapidly changing hardware and workloads, saying people keep trying new points in the design space.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a sign that we haven’t quite figured out the right abstraction yet. People want to write at a higher level than CUDA, but they also want enough control to get really good performance. And where you draw that boundary is still an open question.

For a lot of workloads, you’d like to say, “Here’s the computation on these tiles,” and have the compiler handle the details. But for other workloads, the details—how you move data, how you distribute work, how you overlap communication and computation—are exactly what makes the kernel fast. If the language hides those decisions, it can be difficult to express the optimization you need.

So I see these languages as exploring different points in that design space. That experimentation is useful. The question is which abstractions make kernels easier to write while still letting you get close to the hardware’s performance limits, and whether those abstractions continue to work as the hardware changes.

r001.rationale: The response says we have not yet figured out the right abstraction for GPU kernels.

r002.rationale: It discusses balancing ease of writing with performance, but does not identify training engineers as a motivation.

r003.rationale: It describes the languages as exploring design-space alternatives, but does not clearly attribute their proliferation to rapid iteration on abstractions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a sign that we haven’t quite figured out the right abstraction yet. People want something that’s easier to write than CUDA, but they still need enough control to get good performance. And different workloads need different kinds of control, so you see a lot of experimentation.

For GPUs, the arithmetic is often the straightforward part. The hard part is deciding where the data lives, how you move it, and how you overlap that movement with computation. A useful language has to make those things easier to express without hiding the details that matter for performance.

So I’m excited about the proliferation. It gives us a way to explore that design space. The question is how much of the scheduling and hardware-specific optimization the compiler can handle reliably, and how much the programmer still needs to specify. I don’t think we know the final answer yet.

r001.rationale: The response says we “haven’t quite figured out the right abstraction yet,” directly interpreting the proliferation as evidence that a suitable abstraction has not been found.

r002.rationale: It says people want GPU programming to be easier, but does not identify the difficulty of training engineers to write high-performance kernels as a motivation.

r003.rationale: The response describes experimentation and exploring the design space, but does not attribute the proliferation to rapid iteration on abstractions.
